subtitle: Develop mentoring relationships where both people learn, and sponsor colleagues through advocacy grounded in evidence. You will do this without imposing a cultural role on anyone or bypassing fair opportunity processes.
scope: For DHS leaders who mentor colleagues or advocate for their development. Mentoring is learning support; sponsorship is advocacy within responsible authority, not a promise of appointment. Follow applicable agency, HR, bargaining and data requirements. Use practice material in course activities and never create individual cultural or IDI labels.
introTranscript: A mentor helps a colleague examine a question, practice a capability and navigate relevant work. A sponsor may use influence to make a colleague’s demonstrated contribution visible or support consideration for an appropriate opportunity. Both roles can be useful across differences in experience, role and culture, but neither should require the colleague to imitate the leader or represent a community. This course develops a practical agreement, curiosity, constructive feedback, responsible advocacy and an honest review of the relationship. The employee remains the author of their goals and work. Leaders offer guidance and access within their authority; formal selections retain their approved processes.

lessons.title: Distinguish guidance from advocacy and supervision
lessons.summary: Clarify the role so a colleague knows what support is offered and what remains in a formal process.
lessons.objective: Distinguish mentoring, sponsorship and supervision in a practice work situation.
objectives: Distinguish mentoring, sponsorship and supervision in a practice work situation.
Explain the limit of an informal promise about an employment opportunity.
Identify a relationship question that needs responsible HR or program guidance.
takeaways: Neither replaces supervision or formal selection.
lessons.statement: Name the role before making a promise the relationship cannot support.

image.caption: A useful relationship begins with a clear purpose and role.

intro.heading: Explain what you are offering
intro.body:
A leader may say “I will mentor you” while meaning several different things. They might offer advice, review a work example, introduce a useful contact or advocate for an opportunity. The colleague may hear a promise of promotion or a confidential relationship separate from supervision. Clarifying the role helps both people use the relationship without guessing its authority or limits.

In this course, mentoring means guidance that helps a colleague develop judgment and capability. The mentor asks questions, shares relevant experience and offers feedback; the colleague carries out their own work. Sponsorship means advocacy that makes demonstrated contribution visible or supports appropriate consideration. The sponsor still must respect formal selection rules and the authority of the actual decision-maker.

Supervision carries different responsibilities. A supervisor directs work and handles performance through applicable procedures. A mentor does not automatically acquire those responsibilities, and a supervisor who also mentors should explain where the roles overlap. Do not imply that mentoring conversations are entirely private when the leader has duties or when approved record rules apply.

Set limits on promises. A leader can offer to review an example, introduce a responsible contact or describe relevant capability accurately. They cannot guarantee an appointment outside the applicable process, authorize unapproved compensation or promise secrecy about every concern. Minnesota’s recruitment and selection requirements apply to covered opportunities; seek HR guidance for the actual arrangement.

Differences in role and experience can enrich learning, but they also affect power. A colleague may find it hard to decline advice from a senior leader. Make the purpose clear, invite questions and explain how the relationship can be adjusted. The goal is support that builds independence, not an informal dependency on a powerful person’s approval.

lessons.keyStatement: The relationship should build capability without creating a hidden employment promise.

flashcards.back: Guidance that supports a colleague’s learning, judgment and work goals.
Advocacy that makes relevant capability or contribution visible within responsible authority.
Formal responsibility for directing and reviewing work through applicable procedures.
An exchange in which both people can examine and learn from experience, without assuming equal formal authority.
A clear limit on the role, promise, information or activity in the relationship.

items.title: Advice on a work problem
items.body: The mentor can ask about evidence and options, offer relevant experience and help the colleague choose a next step. The mentor should not automatically perform the colleague’s task or override its responsible owner. Good guidance makes the person’s reasoning stronger rather than making them dependent on an answer.

items.title: Advocacy for an opportunity
items.body: The sponsor can describe relevant demonstrated contribution and help the colleague understand the appropriate process. Advocacy should not make an undisclosed selection or guarantee an appointment. The actual criteria, decision authority and applicable procedures remain in effect.

items.title: A supervisor who also mentors
items.body: Explain which conversations provide optional learning support and which address formal work responsibilities. Follow required procedures and records for actual employment matters. Do not promise that the mentoring label removes duties or makes all information confidential. Seek responsible guidance when the roles create uncertainty.

tabs.label: Mentoring
tabs.body: Mentoring supports a colleague’s learning through questions, examples, practice and feedback. The colleague should gain capacity to do the work, rather than depend on the mentor for a finished answer. A useful mentor can explain how to compare evidence without promising a future appointment. Development support and formal employment decisions have different purposes and authority.

tabs.label: Sponsorship
tabs.body: Sponsorship makes a demonstrated contribution visible through an appropriate introduction or opportunity process. It can counter limited visibility without replacing relevant criteria or selection authority. Describe what the colleague actually accomplished. Inflating their role or privately promising advancement may feel supportive, but it weakens accurate advocacy and creates an outcome promise the sponsor cannot necessarily deliver.

tabs.label: Formal process
tabs.body: Formal authority remains with the roles and procedures responsible for the employment decision. A mentor or sponsor’s confidence cannot confer appointment powers, remove required review or settle a complaint. Explain the distinction early so a colleague can use support realistically. Learning can produce relevant evidence without becoming a guarantee or a hidden alternative selection process.

check.question: A mentor promises that completing a project will guarantee the colleague’s promotion. What is the problem?
check.correct: The promise exceeds mentoring and may bypass the applicable formal selection process; the leader should offer honest guidance and relevant evidence instead.
wrong: Every mentoring relationship automatically gives appointment authority.
A confident promise becomes valid if the colleague agrees.
The colleague should stop doing their own work and rely on the mentor’s influence.
check.feedbackCorrect: Support can build relevant evidence without guaranteeing an employment result outside authority.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Mentoring does not automatically confer appointment authority. A confident promise cannot become valid simply because the colleague agrees. Making the colleague dependent on influence undermines the purpose of developing their capability. Offer honest learning support and relevant evidence, and explain the legitimate process for any future opportunity.

items.text: Help a colleague examine the evidence behind a recommendation.
Describe a colleague’s demonstrated analysis capability to an authorized opportunity owner.
Apply the current appointment process for a covered position.
Offer feedback on a practice briefing.
Introduce a useful contact with the colleague’s agreement and an accurate purpose.
Conduct a formal performance review through required procedures.

lessons.next: Next, agree on goals and boundaries together.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Senior leader Greta offers to mentor Darius and says she will ensure he gets the next supervisory role. Darius believes the relationship has replaced the formal application process. Greta can offer guidance but does not control appointment authority.
options: That her informal promise outranks every selection requirement.
That Darius must adopt her style to receive support.
The learning and advocacy she can offer, the limits of her authority and the actual process for future opportunities.
responses: Informal influence does not replace applicable selection rules.
Imitation is not the purpose of developmental support.
This makes the relationship honest and helps Darius pursue his goals through appropriate evidence and procedures.

lessons.transfer: Describe a practice support relationship in three sentences: guidance offered, advocacy possible and formal responsibilities that remain elsewhere.

move.control: You can clarify your role and make only promises within responsible authority.
move.failure: The relationship becomes an unspoken appointment promise or a dependency on the leader’s favor.
move.next: At the beginning of the next mentoring relationship, state its purpose and limits explicitly.

lessons.title: Agree on goals without imposing a career path
lessons.summary: Develop a practical learning agreement that respects the colleague’s goals, choice and boundaries.
lessons.objective: Write a learning goal connected to a capability the colleague wants to develop.
objectives: Write a learning goal connected to a capability the colleague wants to develop.
Identify an imposed assumption about the colleague’s preferred career path.
Create an agreement with activities, time, boundaries and a review point.
takeaways: The colleague’s goals guide the relationship.
Specific practice is more useful than general ambition.
lessons.statement: Support a person’s goals rather than assuming that growth means becoming like you.

image.caption: A learning agreement gives the relationship a practical purpose.

intro.heading: Ask what the colleague wants to develop
intro.body:
A senior leader may assume that everyone wants the same career path they chose. They may encourage management when the colleague wants deeper technical expertise, or assume that an employee with an unfamiliar style lacks ambition. A mentoring agreement should begin with the colleague’s goals and a capability that can be practiced. Growth can involve different forms of contribution without becoming a ranking of people.

Ask what the colleague wants to be better able to do. A goal such as “explain an evidence-based recommendation to a mixed audience” can lead to useful practice and feedback. A broad instruction to “be more senior” leaves the desired work unclear. Connect the goal to appropriate responsibilities and available opportunities, while avoiding a promise of selection or advancement.

Agree on a manageable activity. The colleague could prepare a practice briefing, reflect on a shareable work example or practice a meeting introduction. Confirm what materials can be shared and how actual records are handled. Do not ask for private client, personnel or medical information simply to make the exercise realistic.

Set expectations for time and communication within approved arrangements. Explain how to prepare, how feedback will be offered and when the relationship will be reviewed. These are optional planning choices, not agency-wide deadlines. If work time, formal program participation or employment conditions raise questions, seek the responsible process rather than making an informal exception.

Invite adjustment. A goal may change as the colleague learns more, and a pairing may not provide the needed support. A respectful route to revise or end the arrangement reduces pressure created by seniority. Declining optional advice should not become a hidden employment penalty. The agreement supports independent judgment and useful learning; it should not make the leader the owner of the person’s career.

Where a mentor, sponsor or supporting leader is a manager or supervisor, MMB Policy 1436 requires immediate reporting of protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to human resources or the agency Affirmative Action Officer. Follow current agency procedures and appropriate information handling. A support relationship or group discussion cannot postpone the duty, replace the formal route or promise absolute confidentiality.

lessons.keyStatement: The agreement belongs to the learning relationship, not to the mentor’s preferred image of success.

items.title: The mentor selects the career goal
items.body: Offer experience and explain options, but ask what the colleague wants to pursue. A different goal is not evidence of low ambition. Keep formal role expectations clear while allowing optional development to reflect the person’s interests and actual work context.

items.title: The goal is too broad
items.body: Translate “be strategic” into a capability that can be practiced, such as comparing options against evidence and naming the decision needed. Explain the task and useful result. A concrete goal gives feedback a basis without requiring the colleague to imitate a personality or communication style.

items.title: The relationship is difficult to change
items.body: A power difference can make adjustment feel risky. Agree on a review and a respectful route to change the activity or pairing. Do not make optional participation a condition of future fair treatment. Formal program rules, if applicable, should be explained rather than invented.

tabs.label: Goal
tabs.body: A goal should come from the colleague’s actual interests and work needs. Someone may want deeper technical expertise rather than a management role. Ask what capability matters and how it would be useful. Assuming a path from identity, age or resemblance to the mentor narrows the discussion before the colleague can describe what meaningful growth looks like.

tabs.label: Practice
tabs.body: Practice turns the goal into a manageable opportunity to act and receive feedback. For analytical development, use a shareable or practice brief and a bounded comparison task. Confirm any required time arrangements rather than relying on invisible extra labor. The task should reveal the colleague’s reasoning, not merely whether they can reproduce the mentor’s preferred wording.

tabs.label: Boundary
tabs.body: A boundary explains responsibilities, information handling and how to adjust the relationship. Do not promise absolute confidentiality when formal duties may apply. A mentor who is also a manager or supervisor must immediately report protected-class harassment or discrimination allegations or incidents to HR or the agency Affirmative Action Officer under Policy 1436. Explain these limits without requiring private disclosure to participate.

check.question: A colleague wants to deepen technical expertise, but the mentor insists that management is the only meaningful growth. What should change?
check.correct: Explore the colleague’s goal and agree on a relevant capability and practice activity rather than imposing the mentor’s career path.
wrong: Label the colleague unambitious for choosing a different contribution.
Require the colleague to copy the mentor’s career history.
Promise a management appointment before any formal process.
check.feedbackCorrect: This supports growth through the colleague’s own goals while retaining realistic work and authority boundaries.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Calling the colleague unambitious treats a different goal as a personal defect. Requiring the mentor’s career path removes ownership of the learning purpose. Promising a management appointment bypasses future authority. Explore the colleague’s intended contribution and select a relevant capability and practice activity without prescribing or guaranteeing a career outcome.

items.text: Practice explaining a recommendation and its evidence to a mixed audience.
Everyone who wants growth must become a manager.
Use practice material and review the arrangement at an agreed point.
Develop a clearer method for comparing policy options.
A quiet colleague cannot be interested in leadership.
Confirm approved time arrangements and privacy limits.

lessons.next: Next, examine assumptions and learn across difference.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Mentor Victor proposes a management goal for Hana, who wants to strengthen specialist research skills. Victor calls that choice a lack of ambition. Hana would value feedback on comparing evidence and communicating limits.
options: Agree on Hana’s research capability goal, choose suitable practice and explain the relationship boundaries.
Continue insisting on management because his experience is broader.
End all support because Hana’s goal differs from his.
responses: This uses Victor’s experience to support Hana’s chosen growth rather than impose his path.
Experience can offer perspective without becoming authority over another person’s optional goal.
A different goal is not a reason to withdraw fair developmental support.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice learning agreement with a colleague-chosen capability, activity, feedback, approved time question, privacy boundary and review point.

move.control: You can offer options and help make a chosen goal practical without owning another person’s career.
move.failure: The agreement rewards imitation and treats a different goal as low commitment.
move.next: Ask the next colleague what capability they want to develop before proposing your preferred path.

lessons.title: Learn across difference without assigning a cultural script
lessons.summary: Use curiosity and perspective checking while avoiding stereotypes, representative burdens and individual developmental labels.
lessons.objective: Identify an assumption about a colleague’s communication or experience.
objectives: Identify an assumption about a colleague’s communication or experience.
Write a question that checks meaning without making the person represent a group.
Distinguish learning from licensed assessment or personnel labeling.
takeaways: Ask about the situation and the person’s meaning.
Shared identity does not mean shared experience.
Do not infer an individual IDI position.
lessons.statement: Curiosity asks what this colleague means; a stereotype assumes what people like them mean.

image.caption: Perspective checking begins with a specific question and a willingness to revise an assumption.

intro.heading: Make difference a question rather than a conclusion
intro.body:
A mentoring relationship across difference can help both people notice assumptions they would otherwise miss. It can also reproduce a stereotype when the mentor treats a colleague as a source of information about an entire community. A person’s identity may be meaningful to their experience, but it does not provide a complete script for their communication, values or goals. Ask about the actual situation and the meaning the colleague chooses to explain.

Begin with your interpretation. A mentor may read a pause as uncertainty, a direct question as disrespect or a written response as avoidance. Identify the observed action separately from the explanation you supplied. Then ask a neutral question: “How did you understand that request?” or “What made that response useful in the situation?” Leave room for a reason unrelated to culture.

Share your own perspective as a perspective, not as the standard everyone must adopt. You might explain why a particular audience needs a concise recommendation while also asking whether another communication route could achieve the same result. Adaptation should preserve accuracy, respect and work requirements. It does not mean agreeing with every approach or ignoring a harmful interaction.

Avoid representative burdens. Do not ask the colleague to explain what everyone from their background believes, or require personal disclosure to make the relationship educational. Use established learning resources and appropriate expertise for broader questions. If the colleague voluntarily shares an experience, treat it as their account rather than a universal finding.

The Intercultural Development Continuum is a learning reference, and licensed IDI assessment remains professionally administered. This relationship does not diagnose the colleague’s orientation or create a personnel score. Reflect on assumptions and try a better work practice without attaching hidden labels to individuals. The useful result is more thoughtful interaction and stronger judgment, not a claim that a person has been placed on a continuum.

lessons.keyStatement: Examine your interpretation before treating it as the colleague’s intent or culture.

items.title: A pause means the person lacks judgment
items.body: The pause could reflect thought, an unclear request, a communication preference or another reason. Ask about the situation rather than guessing. The work may still require a timely response; explain that requirement clearly and examine an appropriate way to meet it.

items.title: A direct question means disrespect
items.body: Check the words, context and work effect. A respectful challenge can strengthen analysis, while harmful conduct still requires appropriate handling. Do not use culture to excuse a real concern or use unfamiliar style to invent one. Ask for meaning and keep formal expectations clear.

items.title: One account explains a community
items.body: A voluntary personal account can deepen understanding without representing everyone. Preserve the person’s choice and avoid assigning additional cultural labor. Broader claims need appropriate evidence and expertise, not an employee’s identity used as a shortcut.

tabs.label: Notice
tabs.body: Notice separates an observable response from the interpretation supplied by the mentor. “The colleague paused before answering” is different from “they lack confidence.” Several explanations may fit the event. Keeping the distinction visible creates a specific question to explore rather than treating a first impression as an established cultural explanation.

tabs.label: Ask
tabs.body: Ask invites the colleague’s meaning without requiring an identity story. A neutral question about what they considered can reveal a task concern, communication preference or missing context. Asking why their whole community is quiet turns one event into a group script. No conversation or attendance record supplies grounds to infer an individual IDI orientation.

tabs.label: Adapt
tabs.body: Adapt chooses a response that preserves the work requirement while improving understanding. The colleague might benefit from clearer context or a chance to organize their reasoning before discussion. Check the effect rather than prescribing imitation of the mentor’s style. Adaptation follows the actual situation; it is not a fixed communication recipe assigned by identity.

check.question: A mentor interprets a colleague’s quiet response as lack of confidence. What is the best first step?
check.correct: Separate the observed response from the interpretation and ask a neutral question about the situation and intended meaning.
wrong: Assign the colleague an IDI orientation from the interaction.
Ask the colleague to explain why their whole community is quiet.
Require the colleague to imitate the mentor’s speaking style immediately.
check.feedbackCorrect: This checks meaning and leaves room for different explanations without personal assessment or stereotypes.
check.feedbackIncorrect: One quiet response cannot establish an individual IDI orientation. Asking someone to account for a whole community imposes a group stereotype and representational burden. Immediate imitation may erase the situation before its meaning is understood. Separate observation from interpretation and ask a neutral question about the actual work interaction.

items.text: Ask how the colleague understood the request in that situation.
Everyone with that background avoids disagreement.
A pause is used to assign the colleague an IDI position.
Describe the words and ask what the colleague intended.
One personal account becomes a claim about an entire community.
An inferred orientation is added to an informal employee record.

lessons.next: Next, provide feedback that develops judgment rather than imitation.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Mentor Dalia reads Owen’s written follow-up as avoidance because she prefers immediate discussion. Owen explains that the written format helped him distinguish confirmed findings from open questions. The task requires accurate, timely information, not one prescribed social style.
options: Insist that written follow-up always proves avoidance.
Review whether the format met the work requirement, discuss a suitable timing agreement and revise the unsupported assumption.
Assign Owen a developmental orientation based on the exchange.
responses: This makes a preference into an explanation without examining the work.
This connects meaning, evidence and adaptation while retaining the task requirement.
A mentoring interaction is not a licensed assessment or personnel label.

lessons.transfer: Describe an invented interaction with observation, initial interpretation, neutral question and an adapted response that still meets the work requirement.

move.control: You can examine your interpretation and ask about meaning without demanding identity disclosure.
move.failure: Difference becomes a stereotype or a hidden assessment instead of a chance to improve interaction.
move.next: In the next learning conversation, check one interpretation before giving advice based on it.

lessons.title: Offer feedback that strengthens independent judgment
lessons.summary: Use evidence, questions and practice rather than taking over the colleague’s work or requiring imitation.
lessons.objective: Write feedback tied to an observed work feature and its effect.
objectives: Write feedback tied to an observed work feature and its effect.
Ask a question that helps a colleague compare options.
Distinguish demonstration and support from completing the task for the learner.
takeaways: The colleague performs and revises the work.
lessons.statement: The goal is a colleague who can make a better-supported decision without you.

image.caption: Guidance builds capability when the colleague can practice and revise.

intro.heading: Help the person think through the work
intro.body:
A mentor may want to be useful by supplying the answer immediately. That can solve one problem while leaving the colleague dependent on the mentor’s judgment. Another mentor may give broad advice such as “be strategic” without explaining how to act. Useful feedback sits between these extremes: it makes the reasoning visible, connects it to the work and gives the colleague a chance to practice.

Ask the colleague to describe the decision question, evidence, options and uncertainty. Do not turn the conversation into a test designed to expose ignorance. The purpose is to understand the reasoning and identify where guidance would help. A question such as “what evidence would change your recommendation?” can reveal a useful next research step.

Give feedback through a specific example. Name the feature, its effect and a possible next action. If a briefing treats an open question as a confirmed finding, explain why that affects the reader’s decision. Invite a revision that distinguishes the two. Avoid an overall personality label or a demand to copy the mentor’s preferred voice when another approach can meet the task.

Demonstration can help when the colleague lacks a model. Show a bounded example and explain your reasoning, then return the practice to the colleague. Do not complete an entire product and record it as their demonstrated capability. Actual work still belongs to its responsible owner and review process; a mentor cannot authorize access or decisions outside the person’s role.

Review the revised work and the learning. Ask what the colleague would do next time and where support remains useful. A mistake can become evidence for practice, while serious formal concerns retain their responsible procedures. The relationship should build the person’s own capability and confidence in sound reasoning, not a dependency on approval or imitation.

lessons.keyStatement: A useful mentor makes the reasoning visible and returns the work to the colleague.

accordion.heading: Choose the right form of support

items.title: The colleague needs a model
items.body: Provide an appropriate practice or shareable example and explain why it works. Demonstrate a bounded step rather than silently replacing the whole task. Then ask the colleague to apply the reasoning to their own example and examine the result together.

items.title: The colleague has several options
items.body: Ask what each option addresses, which evidence supports it and what remains uncertain. Share relevant experience without pretending your past situation is identical. Help the person develop criteria for choosing, while the actual decision remains with its authorized owner.

items.title: The draft has a material error
items.body: Explain the specific issue and work effect clearly. Respectful guidance does not mean hiding an error to preserve comfort. Arrange an appropriate revision and review, and follow formal procedures if the issue requires them. Do not convert one mistake into a permanent cultural or potential label.

tabs.label: Evidence
tabs.body: Evidence identifies a supported feature of the work. A recommendation without a rationale gives the mentor a concrete place to begin; a broad label about potential does not. Use appropriate material and distinguish the colleague’s actual contribution from help others supplied. This makes the feedback examinable without guessing motivation or personal character.

tabs.label: Reasoning
tabs.body: Reasoning explains why the feature matters and invites the colleague’s analysis. Ask how they chose evidence and what another option would change. A demonstration can help, but it should make the decision process visible. Rewriting everything may produce a polished document while leaving the colleague unable to perform the analysis independently.

tabs.label: Practice
tabs.body: Practice gives the colleague a bounded revision and another chance to explain the choice. The mentor provides useful feedback without replacing their work. Neither copying every phrase nor withholding all assistance establishes independence. Development is visible when the colleague can apply the reasoning to a new task and use support appropriately.

check.question: A mentor rewrites the entire analysis and calls it the colleague’s demonstrated learning. What should change?
check.correct: Use a bounded demonstration if helpful, explain the reasoning and give the colleague a chance to perform and revise the analysis through appropriate review.
wrong: Keep the claim because the finished product is good.
Require the colleague to copy every phrase to prove loyalty.
Avoid giving any feedback so the colleague becomes independent instantly.
check.feedbackCorrect: Capability is developed and demonstrated through the colleague’s actual practice, with useful support and clear responsibility.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A good substituted product establishes the mentor’s work, not the colleague’s learning. Requiring copied phrases tests imitation or loyalty rather than judgment. Withholding all feedback does not create instant independence. Explain a bounded example if useful, then let the colleague perform, revise and explain the analysis with appropriate support.

items.text: Ask which evidence would change the recommendation and review the colleague’s next step.
Complete the whole task and report it as the colleague’s capability.
Tell the colleague to be more strategic without an example.
Explain a bounded model and ask the colleague to apply it.
Require copying the mentor’s answer without understanding it.
Praise polish without discussing accuracy or usefulness.

lessons.next: Next, advocate responsibly for contribution and access.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Mentor Rafael sees an unclear recommendation in Suri’s draft. He replaces the entire document and says she has mastered the capability. Suri cannot explain why the recommendation changed and still needs a usable way to compare options.
options: Explain the decision criteria, demonstrate a bounded comparison and ask Suri to revise and explain her own recommendation.
Continue writing Suri’s analyses so every product is polished.
Tell Suri that asking about the reasoning shows poor potential.
responses: This makes the reasoning visible and creates an actual practice-and-feedback opportunity.
Substitution can produce work without developing the colleague’s capability.
A learning question should not become an unsupported personal label.

lessons.transfer: Give feedback on a practice recommendation with observed feature, effect, reasoning question and revision. Include a bounded demonstration only if it helps.

move.control: You can ask useful questions, demonstrate appropriately and give specific feedback without taking over the work.
move.failure: The relationship produces polished products but not independent capability.
move.next: In the next feedback conversation, ask the colleague to explain a revised decision in their own terms.

lessons.title: Advocate with evidence and preserve fair access
lessons.summary: Make contribution visible without confidential favoritism, inflated claims or appointment promises.
lessons.objective: Write an accurate advocacy statement tied to demonstrated capability.
objectives: Write an accurate advocacy statement tied to demonstrated capability.
Identify sponsorship that bypasses a formal opportunity process.
Explain an introduction or nomination transparently within responsible authority.
takeaways: Formal criteria and processes remain intact.
The colleague should understand what is being shared.
lessons.statement: Responsible sponsorship opens a legitimate door; it does not secretly decide who may walk through it.

image.caption: Evidence-based advocacy can make contribution visible without guaranteeing selection.

intro.heading: Use influence responsibly
intro.body:
A leader’s network can make a colleague’s work visible beyond their immediate team. That influence can support development, but it can also create a private route unavailable to others. Responsible sponsorship describes actual capability and uses appropriate opportunity processes. It does not inflate achievements, conceal the decision basis or promise that formal criteria will be waived.

Begin with accurate evidence. What did the colleague do, what capability does it demonstrate and why is it relevant to the opportunity? A statement such as “she clarified conflicting evidence and identified a usable decision question in this review” is stronger than “she reminds me of myself.” Do not claim work the colleague did not perform or disclose private personnel information as promotional material.

Discuss the proposed advocacy with the colleague where appropriate. Explain the introduction, information and purpose. The colleague may not want a particular path or public profile. Avoid assuming that greater visibility is always their goal. Use approved sharing and formal nomination requirements for actual opportunities; the course does not create a consent form or override agency procedures.

Preserve fair access and selection. If the opportunity has an application, criteria or authorized nomination process, use it. A sponsor can support consideration without privately settling the outcome. Minnesota’s covered selections retain the recruitment and selection rules, and other arrangements may need HR guidance. Do not advocate solely on protected identity or invent an appointment exception.

Review your own pattern of advocacy. Are you recognizing only familiar people or public presenters? Are less visible contributions accurately described? This is a process question to examine, not a reason to make identity-based selection promises. Make the basis of advocacy relevant, transparent to responsible roles and bounded by actual authority.

lessons.keyStatement: Advocacy is credible when the evidence is accurate and the decision process remains fair.

items.title: The claim is based on resemblance
items.body: A colleague reminding you of your younger self is not capability evidence. Identify the actual work and its relevance. Experience can guide an inquiry, but familiarity should not be the deciding explanation offered to an opportunity owner.

items.title: The opportunity is settled privately
items.body: If a formal process applies, sponsorship cannot replace it. Explain the relevant contribution through the appropriate route and preserve the decision-maker’s authority. Avoid staging an application process after privately promising the outcome. Seek HR guidance for uncertain arrangements.

items.title: The colleague’s goal is assumed
items.body: An introduction can be useful and still not fit the person’s priorities. Explain what you propose to share and ask about the goal where appropriate. Do not make declining optional visibility a mark against the colleague’s commitment or future fair treatment.

tabs.label: Claim
tabs.body: A claim makes a real contribution visible: explain the colleague’s relevant action, result and limits. “They have enormous potential” may be encouraging but gives a decision-maker little evidence. Accurate specificity supports advocacy without inflating the person’s role. Do not use unnecessary private personnel information to make a recommendation seem persuasive.

tabs.label: Route
tabs.body: A route identifies the legitimate introduction, nomination or selection process. A sponsor can support appropriate consideration while preserving criteria, records and authority. A private promise based on familiarity bypasses those responsibilities. If an opportunity has formal requirements, use the responsible process rather than describing influence as permission to waive them.

tabs.label: Choice
tabs.body: Choice keeps the colleague’s goals in view. Explain the purpose of a proposed introduction or opportunity where appropriate and do not assume management is their desired future. Consent to one conversation is not a commitment to every career plan the sponsor imagines. Helpful advocacy supports informed consideration without guaranteeing or prescribing the final outcome.

check.question: Which sponsorship statement is best supported?
check.correct: Describe the colleague’s actual relevant contribution and support appropriate consideration through the established opportunity process without guaranteeing selection.
wrong: Promise the role privately because the colleague is similar to the sponsor.
Inflate the colleague’s contribution to overcome the criteria.
Share private personnel details to make the recommendation more persuasive.
check.feedbackCorrect: This makes capability visible while preserving accuracy, privacy and the legitimate decision process.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Similarity to the sponsor cannot justify a private role promise. Inflating contributions makes the evidence less trustworthy. Sharing unnecessary personnel details creates privacy risks without strengthening job-related reasoning. Describe the actual contribution and support consideration through the established process, keeping the colleague’s choice and final authority clear.

items.text: Describe how the colleague organized evidence for the relevant review.
Promise the appointment before the approved selection process.
Claim the colleague completed analysis performed by someone else.
Use the established nomination route with relevant information.
Tell other applicants the decision is already made informally.
Include confidential employment details in a promotional introduction.

lessons.next: Next, review whether the relationship develops capability and usable access.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Sponsor Alina wants to recommend Ben for a project. She plans to say he completed the whole analysis, although he led only the evidence summary, and privately promises him selection. The project has an established interest and review route.
options: Keep the exaggeration because advocacy should be enthusiastic.
Describe Ben’s actual contribution, discuss the relevant opportunity and use its established route without a selection promise.
Avoid all advocacy because formal criteria exist.
responses: Enthusiasm does not justify inaccurate claims or a process bypass.
This uses influence responsibly and keeps the evidence and decision route credible.
Responsible advocacy can coexist with formal criteria when its claims and authority are clear.

lessons.transfer: Write an advocacy statement for a colleague with actual contribution, relevant capability, legitimate route, information boundary and no promised outcome.

move.control: You can make relevant contribution visible and support consideration through legitimate channels.
move.failure: Sponsorship becomes concealed favoritism supported by inflated evidence.
move.next: Check the evidence and formal route before the next introduction or nomination.

lessons.title: Review the relationship and improve access
lessons.summary: Assess learning, usefulness and opportunity access without turning participation into a personal ranking.
lessons.objective: Select evidence of learning that reflects the colleague’s own practice.
objectives: Select evidence of learning that reflects the colleague’s own practice.
Identify a limitation in interpreting mentoring participation or outcomes.
Choose one relationship or access improvement with a practical review point.
takeaways: Improve access and adjust the relationship.
lessons.statement: A useful relationship is measured by what the colleague can understand and do, not by dependence on the mentor.

image.caption: A review checks the learning goal and whether the relationship remains useful.

intro.heading: Check what the relationship enabled
intro.body:
A mentoring program can count meetings and pairings without knowing whether people gained useful support. A sponsorship effort can count introductions while overlooking whether the colleague wanted the path or could use the opportunity. Review the relationship against its purpose and the colleague’s own practice, with appropriate information handling. Do not turn optional participation into a hidden score of commitment or potential.

Return to the learning goal. What can the colleague now explain or perform more thoughtfully? Examine a practice or appropriately shareable example and ask how their reasoning changed. The mentor’s finished product is not evidence of the colleague’s capability. A clearer decision question or more accurate account of uncertainty may be a meaningful result even without immediate advancement.

Ask about usefulness and boundaries. Was the feedback specific? Was the time commitment workable? Could the colleague question advice or adjust the arrangement? Did the relationship impose a representative burden or pressure to imitate the leader? Explain how the response will be used and avoid collecting unnecessary private accounts.

Review access as a process issue. Who can discover a current support route, express interest and obtain a suitable contact? A count of pairings does not establish fair access, and a career outcome does not prove the relationship alone caused it. Formal role, opportunity and external conditions may differ. Seek responsible guidance before examining workforce patterns or reporting small groups.

Choose a next step: continue a useful activity, revise the goal, adjust the pairing or strengthen the invitation route. Name the owner and a relevant check. Formal mentoring programs may have their own current requirements; follow them rather than inventing a new agency-wide model. The Equity and Inclusion Operations Consultant can support the analysis while leaders and colleagues carry out their own learning and work.

lessons.keyStatement: Counted activity is not the same as demonstrated learning or fair access.

items.title: Many meetings are recorded
items.body: Meetings show activity, not what the person learned. Ask for a relevant example of the colleague’s reasoning or practice and check whether the agreed goal remains useful. Keep formal participation records accurate while avoiding an inflated claim that attendance proves capability.

items.title: A participant receives an appointment
items.body: The relationship may have helped develop evidence, but the appointment also follows its own criteria and context. Do not claim sole causation or guarantee the same outcome for others. Describe the contribution of support with appropriate limits and preserve the formal selection process.

items.title: A colleague declines the arrangement
items.body: A decline can reflect priorities, fit, timing or reasons the person chooses not to disclose. Do not attach a low-potential label or make it a hidden future penalty. Examine whether the invitation and support were usable, and keep fair access to actual work opportunities intact.

tabs.label: Learning
tabs.body: Learning examines what the colleague can perform or explain through their own practice. Counting meetings records activity, but not the capability developed. A polished product completed by the mentor is also different evidence. Review a relevant work example and the colleague’s reasoning so the learning account reflects actual development rather than participation alone.

tabs.label: Usefulness
tabs.body: Usefulness asks whether the feedback, time and boundaries support the agreed purpose. Offer a respectful way to revise or end an unhelpful arrangement. A colleague need not disclose private experiences to justify an adjustment. Frequency or praise cannot substitute for examining whether the relationship helps them act with greater clarity and appropriate independence.

tabs.label: Access
tabs.body: Access considers how people discover and obtain support through applicable arrangements. Repeated opportunities for a familiar few may warrant a process inquiry, but do not establish everyone else’s motives. Explain evidence limits and possible improvements. Optional mentoring participation should not become an undisclosed personnel ranking, cultural-development label or automatic advancement guarantee.

check.question: A leader counts mentoring meetings and assigns high potential to frequent participants. What should change?
check.correct: Review actual learning and usefulness against the agreed purpose, while keeping optional participation separate from hidden personnel labels.
wrong: Increase the score for people most similar to the leader.
Infer an IDI orientation from attendance.
Guarantee advancement after a fixed number of conversations.
check.feedbackCorrect: This checks the relationship’s purpose without turning activity into an unsupported judgment about a person.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Personal resemblance does not demonstrate learning. Attendance cannot reveal a developmental orientation. A fixed number of conversations cannot guarantee advancement through a separate formal process. Examine the colleague’s actual capability and the relationship’s usefulness, keeping optional participation distinct from hidden personnel labels and unsupported outcomes.

items.text: The colleague explains a revised recommendation using clearer evidence.
Six meetings occurred during the period.
Declining mentoring proves low ambition.
The colleague independently applies the option-comparison method to a practice case.
An appointment followed a separate formal selection process.
Attendance determines the colleague’s inferred cultural orientation.

lessons.next: Use the job aid to build guidance and advocacy that strengthen independent capability.

scenario.context: DSD practice case: Director Nikhil sees that mentoring participants attended several meetings. He proposes a potential score based on attendance and notices that less familiar employees struggled to find the invitation. The records do not show actual learning.
options: Assume nonparticipants have no interest in growth.
Review learning against goals, improve the invitation route and keep optional participation out of personal rankings.
responses: Activity counts do not establish potential and should not become a hidden personnel label.
The unclear invitation means interest cannot be inferred from participation alone.
This examines purpose and access while preserving independent learning, fair treatment and evidence limits.

lessons.transfer: Create a practice relationship review with goal, actual practice evidence, usefulness question, privacy limit and one adjustment with an owner.

move.control: You can check usefulness and improve access without turning the relationship into a personnel assessment.
move.failure: The program celebrates activity while capability, boundaries and fair access remain unknown.
move.next: At the next agreed review point, ask what the relationship enabled and choose one evidence-linked adjustment.

jobAid.subtitle: Guidance and advocacy that build capability without hidden promises.
remember: The colleague’s goals and work remain their own.
Perspective checking is not a cultural diagnosis.
Accurate advocacy preserves fair opportunity processes.

sections.heading: Agree
items: State the colleague-chosen capability and manageable practice.
Explain time, privacy limits, authority and adjustment routes.

sections.heading: Learn and guide
items: Separate observation from interpretation and ask a neutral meaning question.
Avoid representative burdens and forced personal disclosure.
Give evidence, effect and a practical revision.
Use bounded demonstration, then return the practice to the colleague.

sections.heading: Advocate
items: Describe actual contribution and relevant capability accurately.
Explain the proposed introduction or information sharing where appropriate.
Use legitimate criteria and opportunity routes without guaranteeing selection.

sections.heading: Review
items: Examine actual practice and usefulness, not just meeting counts.
Improve how people discover and use support.
State limits on causal or workforce conclusions.
Never infer or record individual IDI orientations or hidden potential labels from participation.
